chapter.title: Arrive, then stop

cards.body: You have led the walk all the way to the viewpoint. Now the only job left is to **stop at the destination and stay there**: say the one sentence you came to say, then go quiet. Picture a guide who reaches the view, points at it, and does not keep shuffling forward into the bushes mumbling "so, yeah, anyway".
cards.simpler: You have walked the group all the way to the viewpoint. The last job is to **stop at the destination and stay there**. Say the one sentence you came to say, then go quiet. Think of a guide who reaches the view, points at it, and stands still. A bad guide keeps shuffling forward into the bushes, mumbling "so, yeah, anyway". Do not be that guide.

cards.prompt: Maya finishes her 3-minute talk on why the team should ship on Tuesdays. Which ending leaves people clearest about where they arrived?

options.text: "So, yeah, that's basically it, I think. Thanks. Any questions, or..."
"Ship on Tuesday, and Friday fires stop happening." Then she stops and looks at them.
"Oh, and one more thing I forgot earlier about the test server..."

whyNot.a: That's trailing off, not arriving: the words fade out, so nobody knows the walk has ended.
whyNot.c: That's starting a new walk, not finishing this one: a late extra point pulls people away from the destination.

cards.reteach: Your close is your one sentence from chapter 1, said once more, then silence. Anything added after it, whether an apology, a shrug or a new fact, drags the group past the viewpoint. End on the sentence and stand still.

cards.title: Rehearse out loud, 3 times
cards.body:
Reading your card silently is not rehearsal. **Rehearsal means saying the words out loud, standing up, at full volume**, 3 times before the real thing. Your mouth has to learn the route, not just your eyes.

Run 1 will be rough. You will lose a step and check your card. Fine. Run 2 is where you fix the sentences that felt clumsy in your mouth. Run 3 should be close to the real one, timed on your phone.

If run 3 is over 3 minutes 30, cut a step. Do not speed up. Cutting is the fix, speeding is the mistake from chapter 5.
cards.simpler: Reading your card quietly in your head is not practice. **Practice means saying the words out loud, standing up, at full volume**, 3 times before the real talk. Your mouth needs to learn the route, not just your eyes. Run 1 will be rough and you will check your card. Run 2 is for fixing sentences that felt clumsy. Run 3 should be close to the real thing, timed on your phone. If run 3 is over 3 minutes 30, cut a step. Do not speed up. Cutting is the fix.

cards.title: Run 3 in the kitchen
cards.body: Dev rehearsed his talk about switching the office coffee supplier while the kettle boiled. Run 1 took 4 minutes 10 and he said "basically" 9 times. Run 2 he cut the whole history of the old supplier, which nobody needed, and landed at 3 minutes 20. Run 3 he said the closing sentence, "Same price, better coffee, one email to switch," and then stood in silence in his kitchen for 3 full seconds, feeling slightly ridiculous. The silence is the part that felt strange. It is also the part the room will remember.
cards.simpler: Dev practised his talk about changing the office coffee supplier while the kettle boiled. Run 1 took 4 minutes 10 and he said "basically" 9 times. In run 2 he cut the whole history of the old supplier, which nobody needed. That got him to 3 minutes 20. In run 3 he said his closing line, "Same price, better coffee, one email to switch," then stood silent in his kitchen for 3 full seconds. It felt silly. That silence is the part the room will remember.

cards.prompt: Your third rehearsal runs 3 minutes 50. Your one sentence is clear and your 3 steps all land. What do you change?

options.text: Talk faster on the real day to shave the extra 50 seconds.
Cut or shorten one of the 3 steps, then run it once more.
Drop the closing sentence, since everyone will have got the point by then.

whyNot.a: That's speeding up, not cutting: the pace from chapter 5 is the thing you should protect, so shrink the route instead.
whyNot.c: That's removing the destination, not the detour: the closing sentence is the one thing you can never cut.

cards.reteach: When a rehearsal runs long, the route is too long, not the pace. Trim one step and keep the opening sentence and the closing sentence exactly as they are. Then run it one more time to check the new length.

cards.title: Close on the sentence, then stop
cards.body:
Your last line is the one sentence from chapter 1, word for word. **Say it, hold still, and count 2 seconds in your head** before you move, sit or say "thanks". Those 2 seconds feel like 20. They are not.

The urge to fill the silence is strong. People add "so, yeah", "that's it really", or an apology. Each one quietly tells the room that you are not sure you have arrived. The silence tells them you are.

Then do it for real, to 2 or more people. A pet or a mirror does not count. Two humans watching is what makes your legs shake, and shaking legs are what you practised for in chapter 6.
cards.simpler: Your last line is the one sentence from chapter 1, word for word. **Say it, hold still, and count 2 seconds in your head** before you move, sit, or say "thanks". Those 2 seconds feel like 20. They are not. You will want to fill the quiet with "so, yeah" or an apology. Each one tells the room you are not sure you have finished. The silence tells them you are. Then do it for real, to 2 or more people. A pet or a mirror does not count. Two humans watching is what makes your legs shake, and that is what you practised for.

cards.body: Priya delivered a sharp talk on a new rota, hit her closing sentence perfectly, and then said "...so, um, yeah, I don't know, that's kind of it, sorry." The room, which had been nodding, looked down. You can spot this mistake in your own rehearsal: if anything comes out of your mouth after the one sentence, you have walked past the viewpoint. Record run 3 and listen only to the last 10 seconds.
cards.simpler: Priya gave a sharp talk about a new rota and said her closing sentence perfectly. Then she added "...so, um, yeah, I don't know, that's kind of it, sorry." The room, which had been nodding, looked down. You can catch this in your own practice. If anything comes out of your mouth after the one sentence, you have walked past the viewpoint. Record run 3 and listen only to the last 10 seconds.

cards.prompt: Which of these is the real sign that a talk has arrived at its destination?

options.text: The speaker says the one sentence from chapter 1 and then goes quiet.
The speaker runs out of things to say and thanks everyone.
The speaker finishes every point on the card, including the extra ones.

whyNot.b: That's running out of road, not reaching the destination: the talk ends because the words stopped, not because the point was made.
whyNot.c: That's completeness, not arrival: covering everything is the opposite of the one-destination walk from chapter 1.

cards.reteach: A talk arrives when the room hears the one sentence you built it around, and then nothing else. The sentence marks the viewpoint. The silence after it tells people they are allowed to look.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **Say it out loud 3 times, cut if it runs long, then deliver it to 2 real people.** End on your one sentence, hold still for 2 seconds, and let the silence do the closing for you.
cards.simpler: **Say it out loud 3 times, cut if it runs long, then deliver it to 2 real people.** Finish on your one sentence. Hold still for 2 seconds. Let the silence do the closing for you. That quiet moment is not empty. It is the full stop at the end of your talk, and the room hears it as confidence.

cards.body: Tonight: stand up, set a 3-minute 30 timer, and do run 1 out loud to an empty room. Record it. Listen only to the last 10 seconds.
cards.simpler: Tonight, stand up and set a timer for 3 minutes 30. Do run 1 out loud to an empty room, at full volume, as if people were there. Record it on your phone. Then listen only to the last 10 seconds. That is where you find out whether you stopped at the viewpoint or kept walking.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now deliver your 3-minute talk to a small group, end on your one sentence, and stop.
